blocks.text: **E-mail** stands for **electronic mail**. It exchanges digital messages over a computer network and can carry text, documents, pictures, spreadsheets, audio and video. A **mailbox** is the storage space linked to an email account. Paper mail is a physical medium, so it is not electronic email.

blocks.title: Milestones
items: **Ray Tomlinson** developed an early ARPANET network email system and used **@** to separate the user from the destination host
**Hotmail** launched, founded by **Sabeer Bhatia** and **Jack Smith**; an early free webmail service
**Microsoft acquired Hotmail**, which later moved to **Outlook.com**

blocks.title: Who invented what?
blocks.text: Tomlinson's 1971 work is the usual answer for network email. His first test message was not preserved; QWERTYUIOP is often quoted but its exact wording is uncertain. Shiva Ayyadurai later wrote a program named EMAIL, but electronic messaging existed before his work. Hotmail was an early free **webmail** service, not the first email system.

On the Internet, email data travels in **network packets** that are put back together at the destination. Email can work over the Internet or over an organisation's internal network. An **intranet** is internal, while an **extranet** permits controlled access to outsiders.
Ray Tomlinson: network email, 1971 | @ separates user and host | Mailbox: message storage | Packet: unit of network data.

blocks.title: Anatomy of student@example.com
rows: The text before @ (here student), commonly called the username.
Pronounced at; it separates the two main parts.
The text after @ (here example.com). Domain names are case-insensitive.

blocks.title: Character rules
items: Ordinary unquoted addresses contain **no blank spaces**.
Letters, digits and some punctuation may be allowed; rules vary by provider.
Standard **Gmail** usernames use a-z, 0-9 and periods, normally 6-30 characters long.
Underscores and hyphens are **not** permitted in standard Gmail usernames.
Uppercase handling depends on the system.
A correctly formatted address does not prove that the mailbox exists.

blocks.title: Length limits (SMTP)
rows: Normally within 254 octets (the SMTP path limit also counts punctuation)

blocks.title: The 320 myth
blocks.text: Adding 64 + 1 + 255 gives 320, but that is not the real address limit; the complete address normally fits within 254 octets. For plain ASCII text, one character takes one octet.
Username first, domain second. An ordinary address has no spaces, and a provider's own limits may be shorter.

blocks.title: Three different terms
rows: Supplies an email account and service.
An application for composing, sending, receiving and organising mail.
A browser interface for accessing an email service; no separate desktop client is usually needed.

blocks.title: Email client examples
items: Clients can store downloaded messages and may give offline access, depending on configuration.

blocks.text: Lycos Mail is another historical webmail example. A service is not limited to one access method: Gmail and Proton Mail offer both web interfaces and applications. **Microsoft Outlook** (the application) is an email program and also a **Personal Information Manager (PIM)**, meaning it handles calendars, contacts and tasks alongside email. **Outlook.com** is Microsoft's webmail service and the Outlook application is a separate product.

blocks.title: Free services
blocks.text: Gmail offers free personal accounts. Tuta (formerly Tutanota) also has a free option. Mailchimp is an email **marketing platform** with a limited free plan, not a conventional personal mailbox.

blocks.title: Who, what, when
rows: Provider **Google**; key developer **Paul Buchheit**; launched **1 April 2004**
Yahoo began in **1994** (Jerry Yang and David Filo); Yahoo Mail launched in **1997**
Founders **Sabeer Bhatia** and **Jack Smith**; launched **4 July 1996**; Microsoft bought it in **December 1997**
Provider **Apple**; iCloud launched **12 October 2011**; works with Apple devices and on the web
Provider **Zoho Corporation**; personal and business email
Russian-origin service from Yandex; launched **26 June 2000**

blocks.title: AOL Mail
rows: Generally dated to 1985, linked to Quantum Computer Services and people including Jim Kimsey, Steve Case and Marc Seriff.
William von Meister was associated with the earlier Control Video business; that predecessor's 1983 history is not AOL's simple founding date.
Verizon ownership is outdated; Bending Spoons completed its AOL acquisition on 2 January 2026.

blocks.title: Company vs mail service
blocks.text: Yahoo the company began in 1994, but Yahoo Mail came in 1997. The desktop Outlook application is not simply a renamed Hotmail; Hotmail later moved to Outlook.com.

blocks.title: Year trick
blocks.text: Order the launch years like a staircase: Hotmail **1996**, Yahoo Mail **1997**, Yandex **2000**, Gmail **2004**, iCloud **2011**.

blocks.title: Five inbox categories
rows: Personal mail and messages not assigned elsewhere.

blocks.text: Primary, Social and Promotions are the common visible tabs, but Gmail supports **five** categories. Which ones you see depends on your settings.

blocks.title: Sidebar options
rows: Messages marked with a star for easy reference.
Messages marked or identified as important.
Messages hidden from the inbox until a time you choose.
Copies of messages that have been sent.
Includes archived mail; excludes Spam and Trash.
Messages waiting to be sent, where the application supports it.

blocks.title: Important distinctions
items: A **star** is separate from the **importance** marker.
**Sent** does not prove the recipient read the message or that final delivery succeeded.
A poor Internet connection may leave a message waiting in an app's **Outbox**.
**Drafts** are saved for further editing; **Outbox** messages are queued for sending.

blocks.title: Trash retention
blocks.text: Gmail normally deletes trashed messages permanently after **30 days**, though you can delete them earlier. Google Chat handles conversations and Google Meet handles video meetings (their visibility in Gmail depends on settings); Hangouts is an older product name.
Drafts: unfinished | Outbox: waiting | Sent: sent copy | Spam: junk.

blocks.title: Message fields
rows: People who should receive a visible copy.
Recipients whose addresses are hidden from the other recipients.
A brief description of the topic.

blocks.text: The system normally supplies the sender details and the sending timestamp. **Cc** means **Carbon Copy**: To and Cc addresses are normally visible to everybody, so use Cc to keep extra people informed. **Bcc** means **Blind Carbon Copy**: Bcc recipients can see the visible To and Cc addresses, but To and Cc recipients cannot see the Bcc list. The sender can see the Bcc recipients in the sent copy, and Cc and Bcc can be used in the same message.

blocks.title: Common commands
rows: Respond to the sender and the relevant visible recipients.
Pass a received message on to someone else.
Add a file; usually a paperclip icon.

blocks.title: Signature is not a digital signature
blocks.text: An **email signature** is a reusable closing block with your name, role, organisation or contact details, which can be added automatically. It is different from a cryptographic **digital signature**.

blocks.title: What is needed to send?
blocks.text: Ordinary email needs a configured sender identity and at least one destination. A subject, an attachment and a non-empty body are not universally mandatory.

blocks.title: The three mail protocols
rows: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: transfers outgoing email and relays messages between mail systems.
Post Office Protocol, Version 3: retrieves messages from a mail server, commonly downloading them for local use; server copies may be kept or deleted depending on settings.
Internet Message Access Protocol: works with a server-based mailbox and synchronises messages, folders and read status across devices.

blocks.title: POP3 versus IMAP
rows: Syncs messages, folders and read status

blocks.title: Exam shortcut, not a rule
blocks.text: POP3 for one device, IMAP for many is only a handy exam shortcut; POP3 is not technically restricted to one device. Both POP3 and IMAP give access to **received** email.

Ports 110 and 143 can support a STARTTLS upgrade, so security depends on configuration. Related terms: **FTP** (File Transfer Protocol) moves files and is not normal email delivery; **HTTP** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is for web communication; **MIME** formats email content but does not send or retrieve mail by itself; **ESMTP** refers to SMTP's extension framework.

blocks.title: Basic recall
blocks.text: Send = SMTP | Retrieve = POP3 | Synchronise = IMAP. Basic ports: SMTP 25, POP3 110, IMAP 143.

**MIME** stands for **Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions**. It extends email message formats so they can represent different content types and non-ASCII text: documents, pictures, spreadsheets, audio, video and multipart messages.

blocks.title: Format versus transport
blocks.text: Calling MIME an extension of SMTP itself is imprecise. MIME extends message **formats**, while **ESMTP** extends SMTP's capabilities.

blocks.title: Multimedia encoding
items: Traditional SMTP was designed for **7-bit text**.
Binary attachments are commonly represented using **Base64**, which uses ASCII characters that are safe for old mail transport.
In simple exam answers the encoding is just called ASCII; Base64 is the more precise example.
Modern SMTP extensions can support more transport capabilities.

blocks.title: Roles in sending and receiving
rows: The system that starts the transfer.
The system that accepts the connection.
The application used to compose, send, read and manage email.

blocks.text: A mail system can act as a server when receiving and later as a client when sending onward. If the sender and receiver use the same system, a separate server-to-server transfer may be unnecessary. A simplified diagram shows two user agents for the two users, but storage and local delivery functions are still needed.

blocks.title: Sending limits
rows: Personal Gmail: recipients in one message (To + Cc + Bcc)
Google Workspace (paid): messages per user in a rolling 24 hours
Google Workspace trial accounts: messages per day
Up to **2,000** total, with no more than **500** external
Mail merge (formerly multi-send): recipients per day on eligible plans

blocks.text: Limits differ by account and sending method and can change. If a limit is reached you may see errors about the sending quota or recipient maximum, and sending may be restricted for up to **24 hours**. Daily message count, recipients per message and the mail-merge quota are three different measures.

blocks.title: Multiplying limits
blocks.text: 500 x 20 = 10,000 is arithmetic only. Creating 20 accounts does not change any single account's limit and does not guarantee delivery.

blocks.title: Attachments and storage
rows: Share them through a Google Drive link.
15 GB shared across Gmail, Drive and Photos.
Limits can vary by edition and administrator settings.

blocks.title: Google Meet
rows: Can last longer; subscription limits differ.

blocks.text: Personal: 500 | Workspace: 2,000 | Mail merge: 1,500 | Attachment: 25 MB | Shared storage: 15 GB.

blocks.title: Protection tools
rows: Pretty Good Privacy: supports encryption (confidentiality) and digital signatures (verify authenticity and detect changes).
Transport Layer Security: used by modern secure connections.

blocks.text: Transport encryption (TLS) protects the connection and does not automatically mean end-to-end message encryption.

blocks.title: Common threats
rows: Unsolicited or unwanted email, often sent in bulk.
Falsifying sender information to impersonate someone else.
Deceptive messages that seek sensitive information or harmful actions.
Phishing through SMS or text messages.

blocks.text: In a typical phishing mail the message pretends to come from a bank or another trusted organisation, asks for confidential information, or sends you to a fake website. Spoofing can support phishing, but the two terms describe different actions. A malicious attachment may install malware, but that is not the definition of spoofing. **Bulk email** means sending messages to many recipients, such as newsletters or announcements: bulk describes **scale**, while spam describes **unwanted** messaging.

revision: E-mail = electronic mail; Ray Tomlinson developed network email in 1971 and chose @ to separate user and host.
Address format is local-part@domain: username first, domain second, no spaces; the real full-address limit is about 254 octets, not 320.
Hotmail: 4 July 1996 (Sabeer Bhatia, Jack Smith); Microsoft bought it in December 1997; later Outlook.com.
Gmail launched 1 April 2004 by Google (Paul Buchheit); Yahoo Mail 1997; iCloud 12 October 2011; Yandex Mail 26 June 2000.
Email client = app (Outlook, Thunderbird, Apple Mail); webmail = browser access (Gmail, Yahoo Mail); Outlook is also a PIM.
Gmail has five inbox categories: Primary, Social, Promotions, Updates, Forums.
Drafts = unfinished; Outbox = waiting to send; Sent = sent copy; All Mail excludes Spam and Trash; Trash empties after 30 days.
Cc = Carbon Copy (visible); Bcc = Blind Carbon Copy (hidden from other recipients).
SMTP sends (port 25), POP3 retrieves (110), IMAP synchronises (143); secure ports 465/587 submission, 995 POP3, 993 IMAP.
MIME = Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions: it formats content; binary attachments use Base64; SMTP is built for 7-bit text.
Gmail limits: 500 messages per day (personal), 2,000 (Workspace), mail merge 1,500, 25 MB attachment, 15 GB shared storage.
Google Meet: personal accounts up to 100 participants; 3 or more people normally 60 minutes.
PGP = Pretty Good Privacy (encryption plus digital signatures); SSL is obsolete, TLS is current.
Spoofing = fake sender; phishing = deceptive request for information; smishing = phishing via SMS; skimming = stealing card data.
